tracks.title: Two gates every toolkit passes
tracks.text: Lesson three point six — verification. A sub-lesson, under toolkit. Two gates every toolkit passes. You just built a toolkit, or imported a stranger's… and the parent lesson told you it's safe to install. Sandboxed. Capability-gated. Signed. [curious] But that answers exactly one question — can this hurt me. It does not answer… does it work. And it certainly doesn't answer the question that decides a toolkit's worth — can an agent use it from the manual alone. This lesson is the two gates that settle all of it. First gate — verify — asks whether the contract is satisfiable. Second gate — eval — asks whether the thing actually works.

tracks.title: Works on my manifest
tracks.text: First — the problem. Works on my manifest. Classic software answers all of this with a test suite that travels in the repo and runs in a build server. But a toolkit's consumer has no build server… and isn't a programmer who reads your test code. And here's the twist that changes everything. A toolkit's primary user isn't a person at all — it's an agent, reading prose. The manual is the interface. [curious] So a passing unit test of the binary proves the wrong thing. It proves the muscle works… [chuckles] not that the instructions teach an agent to flex it. What's missing is a quality check shaped like the thing it's checking. One that travels inside the toolkit… runs without a build server… and tests the manual as hard as it tests the machine.

tracks.title: Two gates
tracks.text: The definition. Quality is two different questions… so there are two commands. The first — verify — asks, is the contract satisfiable. Does it load. The second — eval — asks, does it do the right thing. Picture the two side by side. Verify runs no agent and no model. It prints a board of check marks — files present, exec mode real, capabilities grantable, signature valid — and it can fail on a missing file, an unbuildable command, an ungrantable capability, or a bad signature. Eval is the other gate. It runs one case per eval file — an agent runs, a judge scores — and it can fail when there's no key, a wrong result, a misleading manual, or a case with no task and no eval block. [curious] And the canon — eval is the third leg, beside the skills and the command line. The author proves the toolkit does what its skills claim… and a consumer reruns those same proofs against their own runtime before trusting it.

tracks.title: The structural board
tracks.text: The structural board. Verify reads the toolkit's manifest, parses a descriptor out of its keywords, and runs four families of check. Files present. The exec mode. The declared capabilities. And — for third-party toolkits — the signature. Let me read you a real board, line by line. Line one… manifest present, a check. Line two… skills overview present, a check. Line three is the exec check… exec is command, glyphs not yet registered, build descriptor present — run wb toolkit build. A check, because the source is buildable. Line four… capabilities declared, all grantable, v-f-s and net. Line five… granted by profiles network and posix. And line six… pre checks disabled, two blocks, native bash execution removed. Now picture the decision tree behind that board. It starts at the manifest. Are the files present — if not, a cross. If yes, branch on the exec mode. A command toolkit passes if its binary is registered, or if its build source is buildable. A posix toolkit passes if the binary is on the path. A toolkit with no exec is discovery-only, and passes. Then capabilities — every one grantable, and one profile granting them all together — else a cross. Then trust — first-party skips the signature check, third-party must carry a valid signature or it fails. The failures are verbatim and self-correcting. Not registered and no buildable source. Capabilities not grantable by any profile. No single profile grants all declared capabilities. Third-party provenance, no signature — sign with wb toolkit sign. [curious] Each cross tells you the fix.

tracks.title: Grantable, and grantable together
tracks.text: A depth rung — skippable. Grantable… and grantable together. The capability check is stricter than it looks. It isn't enough that every capability a toolkit declares is known. It must be grantable — and the whole set must be grantable by a single profile. Because a toolkit instantiates under one profile. If no single profile grants every capability it imports… the toolkit can never start. There are four real profiles, a ladder of memory, time, and reach. First — minimal — sixty-four mebibytes, five seconds, and the base capabilities including v-f-s, commands, exec, secrets, and the network sockets. Second — network — a hundred-twenty-eight mebibytes, thirty seconds, everything in minimal plus net, l-l-m, and browse. Third — posix — two-hundred-fifty-six mebibytes, sixty seconds, everything in network plus posix and parallel. And fourth — compute — sixty-four mebibytes, five seconds, v-f-s only. Read it as nested reach, not arbitrary buckets. A toolkit declaring v-f-s and net can't run under minimal — no network there — but network and posix both cover the set. Which is exactly why the green line earlier said, granted by profiles network and posix. Declare a capability no profile lists, and you fail the grantable half. Declare two no single profile holds together, and you fail the grantable-together half. [excited] Both caught before a single instruction runs.

tracks.title: The signature line
tracks.text: The signature line. For a first-party toolkit — one in your own repo — verify skips provenance entirely. Location-trust is fine for code you control. But the moment a manifest declares trust third-party… the rules change. It must carry an author identity and a signature — an Ed25519 signature over the manifest with its signature lines stripped. Verify recomputes that body and checks it. And here's the part that has teeth. Provenance isn't only a verify line — it's a build gate. The build command refuses outright to build an unsigned or tampered third-party toolkit. Refused — invalid provenance. Picture the chain of custody as three moves. First, the author signs once — wb toolkit sign appends an author identity and a signature, so the manifest now carries a cryptographic seal over its own body. Second, the consumer verifies — recompute the canonical body, check the signature. Third, the fork. If the signature is valid, the build proceeds. If it's missing or tampered, the build is refused. Change one character of the manifest and the body no longer matches the signature… so the build refuses. [mischievously] Not by a policy you could toggle — by arithmetic.

tracks.title: The toolkit ships its own exam
tracks.text: The toolkit ships its own exam. Verify proves the contract is satisfiable. It says nothing about whether the toolkit does anything. That's eval. And the shape of an eval is the whole idea. Each case is a single org file in the toolkit's evals folder. One file… one case. No suite means a plain message — add eval files — not a false pass. And the loop is the point. The author writes the cases and proves them green. The consumer reruns the exact same files against their own runtime before trusting the toolkit. The exam travels with the artifact… except this one doesn't need you to read code, because the cases are data, not code. Let me read you the real shipped case from the git toolkit. A headline tagged eval — the agent explains what git status shows. A properties drawer. Task… in one sentence, explain what the command git status shows. Rubric… the answer says git status reports the state of the working tree, mentioning at least staged or unstaged changes, and untracked files. And max steps… two. That's the entire test. No assertions, no harness code. The case dispatches on what it carries — a task makes it the agent-and-judge tier… an eval block makes it the deterministic tier… neither, and it fails with no eval block and no task.

tracks.title: Agent and judge
tracks.text: Agent and judge — the centerpiece. The behavioral test for a toolkit whose interface is its manual… is not a unit test of the binary. It's an agent that has only the manual. Picture the run as a sequence. First, the harness builds the agent's system prompt — the default eval prompt, plus the toolkit's own overview manual injected straight onto it. Second, it hands over the task, with a step budget that defaults to six. Third, the agent reaches for the toolkit's verbs… and the tools answer with outputs, exit codes, and errors. Fourth, the agent calls done — its only escape hatch. Then the harness harvests telemetry — the step count, the unique tools touched, and the error count. And finally it sends all of that to the judge — task, rubric, telemetry, and the result — and the judge returns a verdict whose first line is pass or fail, then one line of reason. The result label reads… check, the case name, in brackets the steps and tools and errors, then the reason. Notice what the telemetry buys. The judge factors execution, not just text. An agent that produced the right sentence but thrashed through six failed tool calls reads differently than one that answered cleanly. [excited] And here's the property no unit test has. The exam tests the manual as much as the muscle. A toolkit whose overview misleads the agent — names a verb that doesn't exist, omits the one that does — fails its own evals. Because the only thing the agent knows about the toolkit… is what that manual told it. [excited] It grades your documentation.

tracks.title: What the judge sees
tracks.text: A depth rung — skippable. What the judge sees. The judge is a second model with one job, and its instructions are verbatim. You are a strict evaluator. Given a task, a rubric, and an agent's result, decide if the result satisfies the rubric. Respond with a verdict whose first line is exactly pass or fail, then one short line of reasoning. The message it reads is a fixed template — and seeing it is what lets you write rubrics that hold. It reads… task, then the task. Rubric, then the rubric. Then a single telemetry line — agent telemetry, steps equals one, tools equals done, errors equals zero. Then agent result, and the result, capped at four thousand characters. The parse is blunt. The first line, upcased, must start with pass — anything else fails. The reason is the next line, cut to two hundred characters. And if the judge errors in transport… the case fails closed. Now the case properties, by default. Task — required — its presence makes the case the agent-and-judge tier. Rubric — defaulting to, the result correctly and completely satisfies the task. Max steps — default six. Exec — default off — set it true to grant host-brokered tools like git and publish, never native exec. And system — an optional prompt override. The rubric-writing rule falls straight out. A rubric is a checkable sentence about the result and the trace, not a vibe. Because the telemetry lists the tools the agent used, a rubric that names the verbs it should reach for is enforceable — the judge reads those tool names right there. Write, mentions staged and untracked state, and the judge can check it. Write, is a good answer, and you've asked a model for a coin flip. [chuckles]

tracks.title: The authoring done-bar
tracks.text: A depth rung — skippable. The authoring done-bar. Verify and eval are the runtime gates. There's an earlier one too — the toolkit-forge's verify skill, the last phase of building a toolkit. It's discipline, not a model. It checks the things a runtime can't. First… that every org source block is balanced — each begin has its end. Second… that every see-also link resolves. Third… that the manifest indexes every skill exactly once, with an overview present. Fourth… that the drawer's identity, binary, and status match the keywords. And fifth… that no file exceeds eight hundred lines — an over-budget skill splits into a thick main file plus references. And the governing rule is the one this whole page is built on. Don't claim verification you didn't do. A recipe that can only be tested where the binary installs gets marked experimental… rather than asserted as verified. Honesty over a clean-looking report — at authoring time, exactly as at runtime.

tracks.title: The disabled tier
tracks.text: The honest part — and on this page it leads, rather than hides. The disabled tier. There are two tiers of eval… and one is switched off on purpose. Tier one is the deterministic tier — a case with a bash eval block and an expect string, which would pass on a clean exit with the expected text in output. It is disabled. Native bash execution was removed from the entire runtime. So a tier-one case reports as skipped — disabled, native bash eval removed. And verify's pre-checks-disabled line is the same removal showing its face on the structural side. The shipped git toolkit's version case is exactly this — a real, correct test that today prints a skipped dot rather than a fabricated green. Let me read you a full run. The summary… git evals, one of one passed, one skipped. Then a dot — version dot org, disabled, native bash eval removed. Then a check — explain dot org, in brackets one step, tools done, zero errors, pass — names staged and unstaged and untracked state. [curious] One tier skipped by design… one tier doing the real work. The lane returns as sandboxed WASM commands, not native bash — that's the honest future. Now the other limits. Tier-two judging is probabilistic — a strict prompt, a pass-fail protocol, and telemetry grounding reduce flakiness but don't erase it. It needs a key — no key, and the case skips rather than lying. And the default models are cheap. None of it is hidden behind a green check. The gate would rather say disabled or skipped out loud… than green-wash a result it didn't earn.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do evals run automatically on install? No — they're a command you run. That's the point — the eval is yours to rerun against your own runtime, on your own key. The author proved it… you re-administer the same files. Who pays for the judge tokens, and which model? You do — eval runs on your key, so no key means the cases skip. Agent and judge default to a cheap model unless you override. A handful of one-sentence tasks costs almost nothing. Can I eval someone else's toolkit? [excited] Yes — that's the entire point. The cases ship inside the toolkit, so you rerun the author's own exam before you trust it. What if my toolkit needs to run commands? Set exec true and the agent gets host-brokered tools — git, publish. What it never gets is native exec. Why did my case fail with no eval block and no task? Because it carries neither trigger — it needs a task to be the agent tier, or an eval block to be the deterministic one. And — is a pass from the judge trustworthy? Trustworthy enough to gate on, not infallible. The strict prompt, the first-line protocol, and the telemetry narrow the room for a sloppy verdict… and because the cases are plain text, you can audit a surprising pass and tighten the rubric.

tracks.title: Back up to toolkit
tracks.text: So that's verification. Two gates, both shipping inside the toolkit. Verify — is the contract satisfiable. Eval — does the thing actually work, judged by an agent that has only the manual. The author proves it… a consumer reruns the same files. [curious] The way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under toolkit — the parent lesson, the three layers this gate guards. From there, commands — the WASM lane the deterministic tier returns on. And agents — the run loop the telemetry comes from. The exam travels with the artifact. You didn't write it to trust it… you reran it.
